pos: n. (a friend of Abimelech king of Gerar, present at the covenant with Isaac; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achuzzath, possession or a holding, from 'achaz, to seize or take hold; named once in Scripture, at Genesis 26:26.
biblical_def: Ahuzzath is named once, as a member of the delegation that came out to Isaac to sue for terms: “Then Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ahuzzath one of his friends, and Phichol the chief captain of his army” (Genesis 26:26). His name means a possession, from the verb to take hold. The word rendered friend here is a court title as much as an affection; he was one of the king's intimates, brought along with the general. What they came to say is the point of the episode, and it is a testimony from the mouths of heathen: “And they said, We saw certainly that the LORD was with thee: and we said, Let there be now an oath betwixt us, even betwixt us and thee, and let us make a covenant with thee” (Genesis 26:28). Isaac had been driven from well after well by these same people, and now their king walks out to him asking for a treaty because the blessing on him was undeniable. The night before, God had renewed the promise: “And the LORD appeared unto him the same night, and said, I am the God of Abraham thy father: fear not, for I am with thee, and will bless thee, and multiply thy seed for my servant Abraham's sake” (Genesis 26:24). The meeting ended well: “And they rose up betimes in the morning, and sware one to another: and Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace” (Genesis 26:31).

corruption_paragraphs: “We saw certainly that the LORD was with thee” is said by the men who had been stopping Isaac's wells. Scripture records such testimony repeatedly — Pharaoh to Joseph, Nebuchadnezzar to Daniel, the centurion at the cross — and it is not flattery. God sometimes compels His enemies to acknowledge His presence with His servants, and the acknowledgment is part of the blessing He promised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God renewed His promise to Isaac in the night and sent the king of Gerar to his tent in the morning, and that a man who has that word behind him may make peace without fear.

pos: n. (a son of Shemida in the tribe of Manasseh; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ani'am, probably lamentation of the people, or I am the people's, compounding a root meaning to groan with 'am, a people; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 7:19.
biblical_def: Aniam is named once, the last of four sons: “And the sons of Shemida were, Ahian, and Shechem, and Likhi, and Aniam” (1 Chronicles 7:19). His name is generally read as the lamentation of the people. His father Shemida heads one of the clans counted in the Numbers census as the Shemidaites, so the household stands in the line of Gilead and Machir within Manasseh — the same register that opens “The sons of Manasseh; Ashriel, whom she bare: ( but his concubine the Aramitess bare Machir the father of Gilead” (1 Chronicles 7:14). What the chapter gives at the end of the Manassite and Ephraimite sections is the geography of the tribe: “And by the borders of the children of Manasseh, Bethshean and her towns, Taanach and her towns, Megiddo and her towns, Dor and her towns. In these dwelt the children of Joseph the son of Israel” (1 Chronicles 7:29). That is the valley of Jezreel and the coastal plain — the richest and the most contested ground in the land, where Megiddo stood and Barak fought and Josiah died. A man whose name means the people's lament held an inheritance in the valley where Israel did most of its weeping.

corruption_paragraphs: Bethshean, Taanach, Megiddo and Dor are not a list of villages; they are the gateway between the sea and the Jordan, and whoever held them held the trade and the armies of the ancient world. Chronicles records that the children of Joseph dwelt there. A reader who skips the geography loses the reason Jezreel appears in every war Israel fought.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God settled His people on ground He chose, and that a man named for the people's lament inherited the valley where much of that lament was uttered.

pos: n. (the head of a house of linen-workers in Judah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ashbea', probably I will adjure, or one who takes an oath, from shaba', to swear; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 4:21.
biblical_def: Ashbea is named once, at the end of the verse that records Judah's guild of linen-workers: “The sons of Shelah the son of Judah were, Er the father of Lecah, and Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea” (1 Chronicles 4:21). His name probably derives from the verb to swear, so that it carries the sense of one under oath. Fine linen in Israel was not an ordinary cloth. It was the material of the priestly garments and of the tabernacle hangings, and it is the figure Revelation uses for the righteousness of the saints. A house devoted to weaving it was a house serving the sanctuary trade. The Chronicler names the potters in the same breath: “These were the potters, and those that dwelt among plants and hedges: there they dwelt with the king for his work” (1 Chronicles 4:23), and he marks the whole cluster with a scribe's aside: “And these are ancient things” (1 Chronicles 4:22). The line goes back to Shelah, Judah's third son by the Canaanitess, whose birth is recorded at Genesis 38:5 — “And she yet again conceived, and bare a son; and called his name Shelah”.

corruption_paragraphs: Fine linen clothed the priests, hung in the tabernacle, and stands in Revelation for the righteousness of the saints. The men who wove it were a named house in Judah, and the Chronicler put them in the sacred record. Vocation and worship are not separate compartments in Scripture: a weaver supplying the sanctuary was doing holy work with a loom.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God named the craftsmen who clothed His priests, and that a man whose name means one under oath headed the house that made the garments of those who swore to serve.

pos: n. (the place where Abimelech dwelt during his war against Shechem; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arumah, probably a height or an elevated place, from a root meaning to be high; named once in Scripture, at Judges 9:41.
biblical_def: Arumah is named once, as the base from which Abimelech ran his campaign against the city that had made him king: “And Abimelech dwelt at Arumah: and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem” (Judges 9:41). The name probably means a height. From there he watched the city: “And it came to pass on the morrow, that the people went out into the field; and they told Abimelech” (Judges 9:42), and he ambushed them. Abimelech was the son of Gideon by a concubine, who had murdered seventy of his brothers on one stone to make himself king, and whose sole surviving brother Jotham had stood on Gerizim and told the parable of the bramble. The book of Judges states its own verdict on the whole affair twice over, and leaves nothing to inference: “Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren” (Judges 9:56), and “And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal” (Judges 9:57). A millstone dropped by a woman from a tower killed him. God repaid both the tyrant and the city that crowned him.

corruption_paragraphs: Judges 9 is the Bible's plainest account of a usurpation and its wages. Abimelech murdered his brothers to take a throne; Shechem crowned him knowing it. The chapter does not leave the moral to be inferred: God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, and God rendered the evil of the men of Shechem, and Jotham's curse came upon them. Political crime is not outside the jurisdiction of heaven, and the account is settled in this life more often than the cynical expect.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God repays both the man who seizes power by blood and the people who hand it to him, and that a bramble king burns the cedars and then burns.

pos: n. (a son of Bela in the line of Benjamin, from whom the Ahohites were named)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achoach, probably brotherly, from 'ach, a brother; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 8:4, and the source of the gentilic Ahohite.
biblical_def: Ahoah is named once, in the Benjamite register: “And Abishua, and Naaman, and Ahoah” (1 Chronicles 8:4). His name probably means brotherly. He was one of the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, whose household is listed in the verses around him: “And the sons of Bela were, Addar, and Gera, and Abihud” (1 Chronicles 8:3), and then “And Gera, and Shephuphan, and Huram” (1 Chronicles 8:5). From Ahoah descended the Ahohites, and that matters more than a bare name, because two of David's mighty men carried the title: Dodo the Ahohite, whose son Eleazar stood with David against the Philistines until his hand clave to the sword, and Zalmon the Ahohite in the roll of the thirty. A clan called Brotherly furnished some of the hardest fighters in Israel. The chapter closes its Benjamite households as it closes all of them: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28).

pos: n. (one of the ten sons of Haman, hanged at Shushan; named once)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning, perhaps given by Hari, or strong; named once in Scripture, at Esther 9:8.
biblical_def: Aridatha is named once, in the roll of Haman's ten sons slain by the Jews at Shushan: “And Poratha, and Adalia, and Aridatha” (Esther 9:8). The name is Persian and its meaning uncertain. The list begins in the verse before — “And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha” (Esther 9:7) — and the book is deliberate in naming every one of them, because the man who fathered them had obtained a decree for the extermination of a whole people. The day had been appointed for the opposite purpose: “Now in the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, in the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, (though it was turned to the contrary, that the Jews had rule over them that hated them;)” (Esther 9:1). And the chapter is careful about one detail that the Jews' enemies would certainly not have observed: “The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” (Esther 9:10). They took no plunder. The deliverance was not a sack.

corruption_summary: The violence in Esther 9 is read as vengeance, where the book records a decreed self-defence in which the defenders deliberately took no plunder.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther 9 is the chapter that most embarrasses modern readers, and the embarrassment usually rests on a misreading. The Jews were under a standing decree of extermination which Persian law could not revoke; the counter-decree permitted them to stand and defend themselves on the appointed day. The text is then careful to say three times that they laid no hand on the spoil, which is precisely what distinguishes defence from plunder. God is never named in the book, and His providence is its only possible explanation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the day the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them was turned to the contrary, and that the men who were delivered refused to enrich themselves by it.

pos: n. (the father of Johanan, a captain of the remnant after the fall of Jerusalem; spelled Kareah in Jeremiah)
etymology: Hebrew Qareach, bald, from qarach, to make bald; the Authorized Version spells the name Careah at 2 Kings 25:23 and Kareah in Jeremiah.
biblical_def: Careah is named as the father of Johanan, the captain who warned Gedaliah of the plot against his life: “And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men” (2 Kings 25:23). Jeremiah spells the same name Kareah: “Then they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah” (Jeremiah 40:8). One man, two spellings in the same English Bible. The name means bald. Gedaliah's charge to these captains was to accept the settlement Babylon offered: “And Gedaliah sware to them, and to their men, and said unto them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you” (2 Kings 25:24). It was good counsel and it was Jeremiah's counsel too. After the murder, fear overruled it: “And all the people, both small and great, and the captains of the armies, arose, and came to Egypt: for they were afraid of the Chaldees” (2 Kings 25:26).

corruption_summary: Fear is treated as a sufficient reason for disobedience, where the remnant went down into Egypt against the plain word of God because they were afraid.
corruption_paragraphs: The last act of the kingdom of Judah is a flight to Egypt, and the text gives the motive without dressing it up: they were afraid of the Chaldees. Jeremiah had told them plainly to stay, and they went anyway, carrying the prophet with them. Fear is a real thing and Scripture never mocks it; but fear is not an argument, and a believer who makes it one will find himself in Egypt.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Gedaliah's counsel to dwell in the land was God's counsel, and that one murder was enough to overthrow it in the minds of men who had already decided they were safer elsewhere.

pos: n. (a trading city named among Tyre's merchants; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Kanneh, of uncertain meaning; named once in Scripture, at Ezekiel 27:23, and generally placed in Mesopotamia near Haran.
biblical_def: Canneh is named once, in Ezekiel's inventory of the merchants of Tyre: “Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad, were thy merchants” (Ezekiel 27:23). It is generally placed in Mesopotamia, in the neighbourhood of Haran, and nothing else is known of it. The chapter is the most detailed commercial document in the Bible, and its purpose is a funeral. Verse after verse lists what came into Tyre and from where: “The merchants of Sheba and Raamah, they were thy merchants: they occupied in thy fairs with chief of all spices, and with all precious stones, and gold” (Ezekiel 27:22). And the self-congratulation of the city is quoted back at her: “The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas” (Ezekiel 27:25). Tyre was the hub of the known world's trade, and the whole catalogue exists to give weight to one sentence at the end of it: “The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more” (Ezekiel 27:36). The cities that traded with her are named so that the reader knows exactly how much was lost.

corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 27 is not an attack on trade. It is an inventory, admiring in its particulars, of a city that had made trade its glory and then its god. The sentence falls not on buying and selling but on a people who said I am of perfect beauty and reckoned their standing by their market. A nation that measures itself by its economy has placed its confidence exactly where Tyre placed hers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ships of Tarshish sang of Tyre and that the merchants of the peoples hissed at her, and that the distance between those two verses is shorter than any trading nation believes.

pos: n. (a man of Geder or Gederah; the title of Baalhanan, keeper of David's olive and sycomore trees)
etymology: Hebrew Gederi, an inhabitant of Geder or Gederah, from gader, a wall or hedge; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 27:28.
biblical_def: Gederite is the title of one of David's stewards: “And over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baalhanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash” (1 Chronicles 27:28). The word means a man of Geder or Gederah, towns of the Judean lowland whose name comes from the Hebrew for a wall or a hedge. The chapter is the inventory of the royal estate, and it is a remarkable passage: the kingdom of David had a named officer over every kind of property. “And over the king's treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel: and over the storehouses in the fields, in the cities, and in the villages, and in the castles, was Jehonathan the son of Uzziah” (1 Chronicles 27:25). Then the vineyards, the olives and sycomores, the oil cellars, the herds in Sharon, the herds in the valleys: “And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai” (1 Chronicles 27:29), and the flocks and the camels, until the summary: “And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David's” (1 Chronicles 27:31).

corruption_summary: Stewardship is spoken of in the abstract, where Chronicles names a particular man over the olives and another over the oil cellars.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 27 is the most concrete chapter on stewardship in the Old Testament. Nothing in David's estate was held in general; every kind of property had a named man answerable for it, down to the oil in the cellars. A church or a household that speaks of stewardship without assigning anybody to anything has the word and not the thing. The chapter's last clause is the theology of it: these were rulers of substance which was the king's, not their own.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a steward is a named man over a named trust, and that what he manages belongs to his lord.

pos: n. (the father of Shaphat, overseer of David's herds in the valleys; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Adlay, probably the justice of the LORD, or lax; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 27:29.
biblical_def: Adlai is named once, as the father of one of David's cattle officers: “And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai” (1 Chronicles 27:29). The name has been read as the justice of the LORD. The verse sits in the register of the royal estate, in which two men divide the cattle between them by terrain: one over the herds on the coastal plain of Sharon, the other over the herds in the valleys. That division is a small picture of how carefully the thing was run. The chapter names officers over the treasures and storehouses — “And over the king's treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel” (1 Chronicles 27:25) — then over the olives and sycomores: “And over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baalhanan the Gederite” (1 Chronicles 27:28), then the herds, the camels, the asses, and last the flocks, with the clause that governs them all: “All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David's” (1 Chronicles 27:31). The shepherd-king kept shepherds, and his Chronicler wrote their fathers' names down.

corruption_summary: Delegation is confused with abdication, where David's register shows a king who appointed named men over divided charges and remained the owner of all of it.
corruption_paragraphs: David did not keep the herds himself and he did not stop owning them. Every charge in 1 Chronicles 27 has a man's name on it and every one of them is called the substance which was king David's. That is the biblical shape of delegated authority, and it is the shape of our own stewardship under God: real responsibility, really assigned, over property that is never ours.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the herds of Sharon and the herds of the valleys had two different keepers, and that God is not served by vague arrangements.
